openingProblem.problem: In 1982 the Soviet Union was a nuclear superpower with no organised opposition. Ten years later it no longer existed. Was the Soviet Union already doomed in 1985, or did it still have a choice?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: in March 1985, was the Soviet system in crisis or only in decline?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: What was wrong with the system by 1982?
chunks.body:
When Leonid Brezhnev died on 10 November 1982, aged 76, he left a state that looked stable from outside and was decaying inside. Tony Judt notes that the Soviet economy had hardly grown through the 1970s and was by the mid-1980s actually shrinking. Oil was the Soviet Union's major export, so when its world price fell from its late-1970s peak, foreign debt rose: it stood at $30.7 billion by 1986. Planning targets were set arbitrarily, shortages were endemic, and without prices or markets no manager had a reason to take initiative.

The official economy was not the whole economy. Shortages created a **second economy** of queues, connections (*blat*) and goods sold "on the side". The economist Gregory Grossman gave it its name in 1977, and Vladimir Treml later put private and semi-legal labour at roughly 10 to 12 per cent of GDP. Seventeen Moments argues that the regime could not suppress this trade without making the shortages worse. This mattered because officials at every level took part, which meant that corruption was built into the way the system worked, not an occasional abuse of it.

On top of this sat the military burden. At its peak, Judt writes, 30 to 40 per cent of Soviet resources went to the armed forces, four to five times the American share, and many Soviet experts already knew this could not go on forever. The leadership itself was old: Brezhnev's failing health had made him the ineffective head of a **gerontocracy** whose own family was involved in wide-scale corruption.

Yet none of this meant collapse was near. Judt's judgement is that the "era of stagnation", held together by fear, inertia and the self-interest of the men who ran it, might have lasted indefinitely, because there was no opposition able to bring it down. Archie Brown agrees that the system was "far from being on the point of collapse in 1985". Gorbachev himself later called the problems of the early 1980s "pre-crisis phenomena". The inheritance, in other words, was a slow decline rather than an emergency, and that is exactly why the choice of leader in 1982–1985 mattered so much.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Economic stagnation was the core problem: the official economy had stopped growing and the second economy filled the gaps.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Stagnation was chronic, not acute: Judt and Brown both argue the system could have survived it for years.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The military burden made stagnation dangerous, because a shrinking economy was paying for a superpower's armed forces.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Soviet experts knew this but nothing forced action; the burden explains strain, not timing.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The system was in decline but not in crisis, so the decisive variable was leadership.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: This underrates how the second economy and corruption had already hollowed out the party's authority.

howItGetsAsked: Examine the problems facing the Soviet Union in 1982.
To what extent was economic stagnation the most serious problem facing the Soviet leadership between 1982 and 1985?

useItInAnEssay.claim: Economic stagnation was the most serious problem the Soviet leaders inherited because it limited everything else they could do.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Judt notes that the economy had hardly grown through the 1970s, while 30 to 40 per cent of resources went to the military at its peak.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that a shrinking economy had to pay for superpower status, so every other problem, from Afghanistan to consumer shortages, became harder to solve.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, Judt also argues that the era of stagnation might have lasted indefinitely, so stagnation alone did not force change.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Stagnation was therefore the deepest problem, but it became urgent only when a new leader chose to confront it.

chunks.title: Andropov: discipline from above
chunks.body:
Yuri Andropov had run the KGB since 1967. In May 1982, with Brezhnev visibly failing, he gave up the KGB to return to the party Secretariat, the better to compete with Konstantin Chernenko, Brezhnev's favourite. When Brezhnev died in November 1982, the party chose Andropov as General Secretary; in June 1983 he also became head of state. He was already 68 and, as Judt notes, not in good health.

His years at the KGB had given him, in Marc Zlotnik's words in the *Encyclopedia of Russian History*, "an excellent perspective" on the depth of the country's problems. He was "much more open than Brezhnev in recognizing the country's problems" but came to office with no plan to solve them. His answer was **discipline**. His regime is best remembered for a campaign against workers who came late or drank on the job, together with minor measures to raise productivity. He attacked corruption at the top, expelling two Central Committee members who had been close to Brezhnev, and he published accounts of weekly Politburo meetings, a small step towards openness.

His most lasting change was in people. Andropov replaced a large number of ministers and regional party leaders with younger men, and he gave the youngest Politburo member, Mikhail Gorbachev, broad authority across the party. Judt confirms that Gorbachev's rapid rise "had been encouraged and facilitated by Andropov". This mattered because the man who would dismantle the system was promoted by the KGB chief who wanted to tighten it, which meant that Andropov's real legacy was a successor rather than a policy.

Time defeated him. Only three months into his tenure his kidneys failed and he went on dialysis; he did not appear in public after August 1983 and died in February 1984, just over a year after taking power. The verdict is therefore mixed. Andropov's methods were those of the old system, order imposed from above rather than reform, and they did not touch the planning system that caused stagnation. But he created, as Zlotnik puts it, a "sense of cautious change", and he raised expectations that the leadership would at last confront the problems it now admitted existed.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Andropov's approach was discipline, not reform: he tried to make the existing system work harder.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: He also began a serious discussion of economic reform and spoke well of innovation in Eastern Europe.

argumentsThatWork.claim: His most important legacy was personnel: younger officials and the promotion of Gorbachev.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: He could not secure the succession: Chernenko, not Gorbachev, followed him in 1984.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Illness and time, not opposition, limited Andropov.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Even with more time he had no plan for the planning system, so his limits were also of method.

howItGetsAsked: Discuss the view that Andropov's reforms were too limited to change the Soviet system.
Compare and contrast the leadership of Andropov and Chernenko between 1982 and 1985.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Andropov's leadership was significant less for its policies than for the people it promoted.
useItInAnEssay.prove: He replaced many ministers and regional leaders with younger men and gave Gorbachev broad authority in the party.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the generation which would launch perestroika gained experience under a leader who believed in discipline, not liberalisation.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, his policies themselves, a campaign against lateness and drinking and a purge of corrupt allies of Brezhnev, left the planning system untouched.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Andropov therefore changed the leadership more than the system, which is why his significance appears only after 1985.

chunks.title: Afghanistan and the Second Cold War
chunks.body:
Two external pressures bore down on the leaders of 1982–1985. The first was **Afghanistan**. Soviet troops had entered the country on 25 December 1979. Judt argues that the invasion was born of domestic anxiety rather than global ambition: the 1979 census showed the largely Muslim population of Kazakhstan and the republics bordering Afghanistan up by over 25 per cent since 1970. A friendly regime in Kabul was meant to send a message to Soviet Muslims. Instead the Soviet army found itself fighting guerrillas, the *mujahideen*, in mountain terrain, against an enemy armed by the United States. Seventeen Moments notes that the war diverted money from a civilian economy that was grinding to a halt and damaged Soviet relations with the West and the Third World.

Judt calls the war "a catastrophe" for the Soviet Union: a decade-long war of attrition and an extended international humiliation. Its deepest consequence came later. Politburo member Yegor Ligachev admitted that after Afghanistan there could no longer be any question of using force in Eastern Europe. This mattered because the Red Army's credibility was the final guarantee of the Soviet bloc, which meant that the war of the early 1980s quietly removed an option the leadership would need in 1989.

The second pressure was the **Second Cold War**. In November 1982, the month Brezhnev died, the United States announced the MX missile; five months later came the Strategic Defense Initiative ("Star Wars"), which Moscow protested as a breach of the 1972 ABM Treaty. In March 1983 Ronald Reagan called the Soviet Union an "evil empire". Judt writes that Andropov in particular took the American threat very seriously and believed Washington was contemplating pre-emptive nuclear war. On 1 September 1983 a Soviet fighter shot down Korean Airlines flight 007 after it strayed into Soviet airspace, killing all 269 people aboard; a serious diplomatic crisis followed.

How much did this pressure matter? It is tempting to say that American rearmament bankrupted the USSR. Judt rejects that as "not quite accurate": the Soviet Union could ill afford the arms race it had begun in 1974, but "bankruptcy alone would not have brought Communism to its knees". The external pressures raised the cost of stagnation and made the old leaders less willing to compromise; they did not by themselves force change.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Afghanistan drained resources and, more importantly, destroyed confidence in Soviet force.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Its full effects emerged after 1985; in 1982–1985 the leadership still fought on.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Second Cold War raised the cost of stagnation and hardened the old leadership.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Judt argues the US build-up did not by itself break the system.

argumentsThatWork.claim: External pressure explains strain, not the decision to reform: that came from inside the party.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: A leader facing a hostile superpower might equally have chosen repression, as Andropov's discipline shows.

howItGetsAsked: Evaluate the reasons for, and the consequences of, the Soviet Union's continued war in Afghanistan between 1982 and 1985.
Examine the impact of the Second Cold War on the Soviet Union between 1982 and 1985.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The war in Afghanistan weakened the Soviet Union most by undermining the credibility of Soviet force.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Judt calls it a decade-long war of attrition and an extended international humiliation, and Ligachev admitted that afterwards force could not be used in Eastern Europe.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the Red Army, the final guarantee of the bloc, could no longer be relied on politically, which narrowed the options of every leader after Brezhnev.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, between 1982 and 1985 the leadership kept fighting, so the war's political consequences were only partly visible at the time.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Afghanistan was therefore a slow-acting weakness rather than an immediate cause of change.

chunks.title: Chernenko and the choice of Gorbachev
chunks.body:
When Andropov died in February 1984, the Politburo did not choose his protégé. It chose Konstantin Chernenko, aged 72, a man who had spent his whole career in party propaganda and administration and had risen as Brezhnev's assistant. According to Zlotnik, this was "a last desperate effort by the sclerotic Brezhnev generation to hold on to power and block the election of Mikhail Gorbachev". Chernenko was so ill that, Judt writes, he could hardly complete his speech at Andropov's funeral.

Chernenko was not without ideas. Before 1984 he had campaigned for more attention to citizens' letters and warned that unrest like Poland's Solidarity could spread if public opinion was ignored. But in office his thirteen months were, in Zlotnik's words, "a period of marking time". The personnel changes and the modest initiatives of Andropov's year halted. In his last months Chernenko was ill and rarely appeared in public, while Gorbachev manoeuvred to succeed him.

Chernenko died in March 1985, and on 11 March the party made Gorbachev General Secretary. He was born in 1931 in Stavropol, had joined the Central Committee at 41, and was twenty years younger than his predecessors. Judt notes that he was "widely seen as a likely reformer", though he was very much an *apparatchik* who had risen through the party. His ideas were already visible: in a speech of December 1984 he had called for a "perestroika of the forms and methods of running the economy".

Why did the party choose him? Partly because of biology. Judt points out that the three leaders who died in quick succession were all born before the First World War; with them a generation disappeared, and the younger men who followed "would have little option" but to address corruption, stagnation and inefficiency. Partly because of Andropov, who had given Gorbachev the experience and authority to win. And partly because the Chernenko interlude showed the alternative: a leadership that could only mark time. This mattered because Judt argues that only a Communist could bring down the system, which meant that the succession of March 1985 was the real turning point of the decade.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Chernenko's election was a holding operation by the Brezhnev generation, and it failed to hold.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Chernenko had shown interest in public opinion before 1984, so he was not a pure reactionary.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Gorbachev rose because Andropov had prepared him and the old generation was dying out.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: His victory was not inevitable: in 1984 the Politburo had preferred Chernenko.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The choice of leader mattered because the system was not in crisis: change had to come from the top.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Gorbachev's early aims were modest, so the choice of March 1985 did not decide the outcome of 1991.

howItGetsAsked: Analyse the reasons for Gorbachev's rise to the leadership of the Soviet Union between 1982 and 1985.
Compare and contrast the leadership of Andropov and Chernenko between 1982 and 1985.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Gorbachev rose to power mainly because the generation that had ruled since Brezhnev was physically dying out.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Brezhnev died in November 1982 aged 76, Andropov in February 1984 after just over a year, and Chernenko in March 1985 after thirteen months.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the party ran out of leaders of the old generation, so the younger men Andropov had promoted became the only credible choice.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, biology alone did not decide it: in 1984 the Politburo chose Chernenko precisely to block Gorbachev.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Gorbachev's rise therefore depended on Andropov's patronage as much as on his rivals' deaths.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: To what extent was economic stagnation the most serious problem facing the Soviet leadership between 1982 and 1985?
essayQuestions.scope: Soviet Union; problems facing the leadership

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far, using degree language
decodeKey.scope: The problems facing the Soviet leadership
decodeKey.judgement: How far stagnation, compared with the military burden, Afghanistan and the leadership itself, was the most serious problem

modelPlan.thesis: Stagnation was the most serious problem because it limited every other choice, but it was chronic rather than urgent; the leadership's age and the Afghan war decided how and when it was confronted.

arguments.claim: Stagnation: an economy that hardly grew and relied on a second economy (named factor first).
The military burden and the Second Cold War made stagnation dangerous.
Afghanistan drained resources and confidence.
An ageing leadership could not act: three deaths in under three years.

modelPlan.counter: Judt and Brown argue that stagnation might have lasted for years, so the leadership problem, not the economy, decided the timing of change.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which problem made the others impossible to solve? Stagnation did, so it was the most serious; but only a new leader could act on it.

segments.text: Economic stagnation was the most serious problem because it limited every other choice the leadership could make.
Judt notes that the economy had hardly grown through the 1970s, while foreign debt rose as oil prices fell, reaching $30.7 billion by 1986.
This meant that the state could not pay for both its military and its consumers, so every other problem, from Afghanistan to shortages, became harder to solve.
However, Judt also argues that the era of stagnation might have lasted indefinitely, which suggests stagnation was chronic rather than urgent.
Stagnation was therefore the most serious problem, but the most urgent one was a leadership too old to confront it.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: “Andropov's reforms were too limited to change the Soviet system.” Discuss with reference to the period 1982 to 1984.

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: test the claim with arguments for and against, then judge
decodeKey.factorOrTask: Andropov's reforms, and whether they were too limited
decodeKey.judgement: How far the claim holds, given what Andropov did and what he left behind

modelPlan.thesis: The claim is largely right about policy, since discipline did not touch central planning, but it misses Andropov's lasting change: the promotion of a reforming generation led by Gorbachev.

arguments.claim: For: discipline and anti-corruption tackled symptoms, not central planning (named factor first).
For: illness and death after just over a year cut his programme short.
Against: younger personnel and the promotion of Gorbachev changed the leadership.
Against: limited openness and a sense of cautious change raised expectations.

modelPlan.counter: Andropov's significance appears only after 1985, so judged within 1982–1984 the claim is correct.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Did his actions change how the system worked, or only who would run it? The second, so the claim holds for policy but not for personnel.

segments.text: Andropov's reforms were too limited to change how the Soviet system worked, but not who would run it.
His regime is best remembered for a discipline campaign against lateness and drinking at work, and he expelled two Central Committee members close to Brezhnev.
This meant that he attacked the symptoms of stagnation, idleness and corruption, while leaving central planning, its cause, untouched.
However, he replaced many ministers and regional leaders with younger men and gave Gorbachev broad authority in the party.
The claim is therefore right about his policies but wrong about his legacy, which lay in the generation he promoted.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the reasons for, and the consequences of, the Soviet Union's continued war in Afghanistan between 1982 and 1985.
essayQuestions.scope: Soviet Union; the war in Afghanistan

decodeKey.verb: Evaluate: weigh strengths and limits, then judge
decodeKey.judgement: Which reasons mattered most, and how serious the consequences were for the USSR

modelPlan.thesis: The war continued mainly because the leadership feared the domestic and international cost of defeat; its most serious consequence was not the cost in money but the loss of confidence in Soviet force.

arguments.claim: Reason: domestic anxiety about Soviet Central Asia.
Reason: an ageing leadership unwilling to admit failure, under Cold War pressure.
Consequence: resources diverted and relations with the West damaged.
Consequence: a humiliation that undermined confidence in force.

modelPlan.counter: Many consequences emerged only after 1985, so within 1982–1985 the war's impact was limited.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which consequence lasted longest? The loss of confidence in force, which shaped Soviet choices in 1989.

segments.text: The most serious consequence of the war was that it undermined confidence in Soviet force.
Judt calls it a decade-long war of attrition and an extended international humiliation, and Ligachev later admitted that after Afghanistan force could not be used in Eastern Europe.
This meant that the Red Army, the final guarantee of the Soviet bloc, lost its political credibility, which narrowed the options of every later leader.
However, between 1982 and 1985 the leadership still fought on, so this consequence was only partly visible at the time.
The war's consequences were therefore more serious in the long term than in 1982–1985 itself.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the leadership of Andropov and Chernenko in the Soviet Union between 1982 and 1985.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, explicitly linked
decodeKey.scope: Their leadership of the Soviet Union
decodeKey.judgement: Which differences mattered most for what followed

modelPlan.thesis: Both were old, ill and short-lived leaders of the Brezhnev generation, but they differed sharply in purpose: Andropov tried to tighten and renew the system, while Chernenko only held the line.

arguments.claim: Similarity: both were old, ill and ruled briefly.
Similarity: neither changed central planning.
Difference: Andropov's discipline and anti-corruption against Chernenko's marking time.
Difference: Andropov promoted younger men and Gorbachev; Chernenko was chosen to block him.

modelPlan.counter: The similarities run deep: both belonged to the generation Judt says was disappearing, so their differences were of style more than substance.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which difference shaped the future? Andropov's promotion of Gorbachev, which made Chernenko's holding operation temporary.

segments.text: Andropov and Chernenko were alike in age and health, but different in purpose.
Andropov replaced many ministers and regional leaders with younger men, whereas Chernenko, chosen in 1984 to block Gorbachev, halted those changes.
This meant that Andropov's year began a transfer of power to a new generation, while Chernenko's thirteen months only delayed it.
However, neither touched central planning, so in economic policy the two leaderships were more similar than different.
The decisive difference was therefore in personnel rather than policy.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the impact of the Second Cold War on the Soviet Union between 1982 and 1985.
essayQuestions.scope: Soviet Union; impact of the Second Cold War

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.judgement: How far US pressure changed Soviet policy and capacity

modelPlan.thesis: The Second Cold War raised the cost of the Soviet military burden and hardened the old leaders, but it did not by itself force change; that came from the succession.

arguments.claim: US rearmament and SDI raised the cost of competition (named factor first).
Fear of a pre-emptive strike hardened the leadership.
Afghanistan tied the Cold War to a draining war.
Judt: bankruptcy alone would not have brought Communism down.

modelPlan.counter: The arms race could be seen as the lever that broke the Soviet system.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Did the pressure change Soviet policy before 1985? No: it raised costs but the reform decision came from inside.

segments.text: The Second Cold War raised the cost of being a superpower but did not by itself change Soviet policy.
The United States announced the MX missile in November 1982 and SDI five months later, while Reagan called Moscow an 'evil empire' in March 1983.

This meant that a stagnant economy already giving 30 to 40 per cent of resources to the military at its peak faced a more expensive race, and that the old leaders, fearing a strike, were less willing to compromise.
However, Judt argues that bankruptcy alone would not have brought Communism down, so external pressure explains strain rather than change.
The Second Cold War's impact was therefore to raise the stakes of stagnation, not to end it.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the reasons for Gorbachev's rise to the leadership of the Soviet Union between 1982 and 1985.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its reasons and show how they connect
decodeKey.judgement: Which reasons mattered most, and how they combined

modelPlan.thesis: Gorbachev rose mainly because the old generation died out while Andropov had prepared him to succeed; Chernenko's interlude showed the party the cost of not choosing him.

arguments.claim: The old generation died out: Brezhnev, Andropov and Chernenko in under three years.
Andropov's patronage gave Gorbachev authority and experience.
Gorbachev's age and reputation as a likely reformer.
The failure of Chernenko's holding operation.

modelPlan.counter: His rise was not inevitable: in 1984 the Politburo chose Chernenko precisely to block him.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Without which reason would he not have risen? Andropov's patronage, because it made him the obvious successor once the old men were gone.

segments.text: Gorbachev rose mainly because the generation that had ruled since Brezhnev was dying out.
Brezhnev died in November 1982, Andropov in February 1984 and Chernenko in March 1985, after thirteen months.
This meant that, as Judt argues, the party had little option but to turn to younger men, and Andropov had already given Gorbachev the authority to lead them.
However, in 1984 the Politburo chose Chernenko precisely to block Gorbachev, which shows the old generation could still delay him.
His rise was therefore made likely by biology but made possible by Andropov's patronage.
